summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's 2015 Penal Code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries up to seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained after independence with an enhanced sentence in the first post-independence penal code, adopted in 2015.

No anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office records same-sex activity as a crime in Eritrea and states that no such protective legislation exists; the UK has raised these concerns bilaterally and through the European Union.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Eritrea and cannot adopt. There is no protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Public expression and association are restricted. A 2023 US State Department report found no public LGBTQ organisations and tight restrictions on the expression of sexual orientation and gender identity, so LGBTQI+ people cannot freely assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship is compounded by heavy social stigma, and in the early 2000s state-run radio and television aired programmes detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality.

Foreign LGBTQ nationals have been removed from Eritrea on the basis of local law. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, a gay Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government called him a "dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country" and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local laws including Article 600 of the Penal Code. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one described as openly homosexual. The Eritrean ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the provisions of law prohibiting homosexual relations, and Italian diplomats condemned the action.

Detention facilities are used against people suspected of same-sex conduct. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, known for housing political prisoners and journalists. Gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military are reported to have suffered severe physical and verbal abuse, and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers, on the basis of a 2002 UK refugee claimant account that is unconfirmed.

Exposure extends beyond prosecution to official and societal hostility. The 2023 State Department report states that openly LGBTQI+ persons risked imprisonment and for that reason did not participate in the political process, and that societal discrimination continues alongside a law making no gender distinction for assault. An Asmarino relay of the 2011 State Department report records societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians and documents the government labelling disloyal individuals as "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles". The 2010 State Department report records criminalisation and societal stigma alongside torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service.

There are no laws banning conversion therapy. OutRight Action International found that conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity are widespread owing to social stigma, and LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time.

Criminalisation undermines health and care access. ILGA and some HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law, arguing it makes prevention programmes directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an area of concern.

The government has rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review recommendation to legalise same-sex sexual activity as "in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people", with no major efforts to change or rescind the existing law. Eritrea joined other African states in rejecting the Yogyakarta Principles in 2010.
tangentialFactors:
Criminalisation sits inside a broader pattern of repression. The 2010 State Department report places societal stigma against gay men and lesbians alongside torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service, and reports of abuse, torture and beating of prisoners are commonplace, with some prisoners allegedly executed. The UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office reported that the death penalty was not used in 2013.

Detention for suspected same-sex conduct has historically been routed through facilities holding political prisoners and journalists, as in the 2003 Adi Abeyto transfers, which places affected detainees in the same environment as those cases drawing international scrutiny.

Diplomatic pressure has not produced legislative change. The UK has raised the absence of anti-discrimination protection and the criminalisation of same-sex activity bilaterally and through the EU, and Italian diplomats condemned the 2004 expulsions, while the government's stated position remains that the law reflects the values and traditions of the Eritrean people.

Health and welfare consequences are recorded by organisations working in the region: ILGA and HIV/AIDS prevention groups argue that the offence obstructs prevention work with men who have sex with men, and US reporting identifies societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an area of concern.
localsOnly:
The offence binds residents and citizens on the same terms as visitors, and no domestic legislative route to protection exists: there is no anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex couples have no legal recognition and cannot adopt.

Residents have no domestic organisations to turn to. The 2023 State Department report found no public LGBTQ organisations, and expression of sexual orientation and gender identity is tightly restricted, so individuals cannot assemble, associate or speak publicly without risking identification, arrest, discrimination or violence.

Charges can be used as a character designation rather than a sexual-conduct allegation. The 2011 State Department report records the government labelling disloyal individuals as "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles", which means the label may be applied to perceived opponents irrespective of their actual conduct.

Those in national service and the military report abuse. A 2002 UK refugee claimant account, unconfirmed, describes gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military suffering physical and verbal abuse and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers.

Residents are offered conversion therapy rather than prosecution in some cases, and OutRight Action International reports that conversion therapy and forced-change attempts are widespread through social stigma; no law bans the practice. No youth-specific care findings are recorded for Eritrea.

Access to health services is constrained by the law itself: prevention programmes directed at men who have sex with men are described by ILGA and HIV/AIDS prevention groups as extremely difficult to run, and societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS persists.

Media available to residents carries state messaging on the subject. State-run radio and television aired programmes in the early 2000s detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality, and censorship of LGBTQ issues is state-sponsored.
outOfScopeNotes:
Source numbering for the offence is unresolved. Outright International and the current inventory cite Article 310(1) of the 2015 Penal Code, while the 2013 Mannina expulsion record and other cited material reference Article 600 of the Penal Code. Whether these are the same provision under successive codes or different citations of one offence is not settled by the available sources.

The 2002 account of abuse against gay and lesbian Eritrean military personnel rests on a single UK refugee claimant account and is described in the source inventory itself as unconfirmed.

No findings on legal gender recognition, gender markers on identity or travel documents, entry or visa screening on the basis of gender identity, or healthcare restrictions specific to transgender persons are recorded in this inventory; their status in Eritrean law is not sourced here.

No youth-specific care findings are recorded. Several entries derive from an encyclopaedia summary of the underlying reports rather than from the primary documents, and the UK Foreign Office country-of-concern report carries a 2015 copyright date, so its statements describe the position as of that year.
